title: Verb-final (SOV) word order
explanation: The verb comes at the end of the sentence, after the subject and object, instead of in the middle.
example_native: 私はりんごを食べます。
example_gloss: I apple eat = I eat an apple.
bridge_note: English fixes the verb in the middle (subject-verb-object), so the eat/action word always comes right after "I." Japanese saves it for last — you often don't know what's actually happening in a sentence until the very end.

title: Particles mark grammatical role instead of word order
explanation: Small words after each noun (は, が, を, に, で...) show whether it's the topic, subject, object, location, and so on — word order alone doesn't tell you.
example_native: 友達に手紙を書きます。
example_gloss: Friend-to letter-[object] write = I write a letter to my friend.
bridge_note: English uses prepositions before a noun ("to my friend") and relies on word order for subject/object. Japanese puts a small marker after the noun instead — the role is glued to the word itself, not to where it sits in the sentence.

title: Verbs don't conjugate for person or number
explanation: The same verb form is used whether the subject is I, you, he, she, we, or they — Japanese verbs only change for tense and politeness level, never for who's doing the action.
example_gloss: Eat(s). — could mean I eat, you eat, she eats, they eat, depending on context.
bridge_note: English still marks this a little ("I eat" vs "she eats"), and Portuguese marks it heavily (como/comes/come/comemos). Japanese drops person-marking entirely — the subject is often left unsaid once it's clear from context.

title: I-adjectives conjugate like verbs
explanation: One class of adjectives (ending in い) changes form for past tense and negation on its own, without needing a separate "to be" verb.
bridge_note: English adjectives never change form — you always need a separate verb ("was") to shift tense. Japanese i-adjectives carry the tense themselves, behaving more like a verb than like an English adjective.

title: は marks the topic, が marks the subject — and they're not the same thing
explanation: は introduces what the sentence is about; が marks the grammatical subject of the action. A sentence can have a topic that isn't its subject.
example_gloss: As for elephants, the trunk is long. (topic: elephants; subject of "long": trunk)
bridge_note: English collapses topic and subject into the same word ("elephants have long trunks" — one subject, one role). Japanese can name a topic and then a separate subject within it — a distinction English grammar doesn't really have a slot for.

title: Politeness is built into the verb form itself
explanation: The same action is expressed with a different verb ending depending on how formal the situation is — plain form among friends, polite ます form with strangers or in public.
bridge_note: English signals formality through word choice and tone ("grab a bite" vs "would you care to dine"), never through the verb's grammatical ending. Japanese makes register a fixed grammatical choice on every single verb, not just a style preference.

title: One verb form links actions, makes requests, and builds other grammar
explanation: The て (te) form is a connector shape every verb has — it links a sequence of actions together, forms polite requests, and combines with other words to build tenses and moods (like the ongoing-action ~ている).
example_native: 朝起きて、顔を洗って、朝ごはんを食べます。
example_gloss: I get up, wash my face, and eat breakfast. (three verbs chained with て, only the last one fully conjugated)
bridge_note: English repeats "and" between each verb ("I get up and wash and eat"). Japanese instead shifts every verb but the last into this one shared connector shape — a single form doing several jobs at once.

title: Relative clauses sit before the noun, with no "that/which" needed
explanation: To describe a noun with a clause ("the book that I read"), Japanese just places the whole clause directly in front of the noun — no relative pronoun, no separate connecting word at all.
example_gloss: the book that I read (literally: I read book)
bridge_note: English needs "that"/"which" to glue the clause onto the noun. Japanese doesn't glue anything — the clause just sits where an adjective would, doing the same job with zero extra words.

title: Many verbs come in matched pairs — one for "do it," one for "it happens"
explanation: A large set of verbs exist in two closely related forms: a transitive version (someone acts on something) and an intransitive version (it just happens on its own), often differing by only a syllable.
example_native: ドアを開ける。 / ドアが開く。
example_gloss: [Someone] opens the door. / The door opens (by itself).
bridge_note: English usually reuses the exact same verb for both ("I open the door" / "the door opens") and lets context sort out who's doing what. Japanese marks the difference with a genuinely different verb, learned as its own pair.

title: Four different ways to say "if"
explanation: Japanese has four conditional forms (と, ば, たら, なら), and they aren't interchangeable — each implies a different relationship between the condition and what follows it (automatic result, general truth, sequential event, or premise).
example_native: 雨が降ったら、行きません。
example_gloss: If it rains, I won't go.
bridge_note: English gets by with one word, "if," for all of these cases. Japanese forces a choice among four forms up front, each nudging the sentence's logic in a slightly different direction.

title: Causative and passive verb forms are built the same way, but mean opposite things
explanation: The causative ("make/let someone do") and passive ("have something done to you") each attach their own ending to the verb stem, and for some verb classes the two endings look nearly identical — only the surrounding particles and context tell them apart.
example_native: 先生が学生を勉強させる。 学生が先生に褒められる。
example_gloss: The teacher makes the student study. The student is praised by the teacher.
bridge_note: English marks causative and passive with completely different sentence structures ("makes X do" vs. "is done to"), so there's no risk of confusing them. In Japanese the verb endings can look close enough that the particle attached to the noun is what actually disambiguates which one it is.
